processing component (judging math problems, the semantics of a sentence, or the symmetry of a geometric figure). In the last practice block (3 trials of set size 2), the tasks were practiced as they were later administered. The second practice block was used to calculate individual time limits for the processing component (mean reaction time + 2.5 SD). These limits were then applied in the last practice block and in all experimental trials, without informing participants of this calibration step beforehand. However, the final task instructions included this information.

Edinburgh Inventory

To assess handedness, participants filled out the ten-item German version of the Edinburgh Inventory 34 . Participants indicated which hand they typically use to perform activities (e.g., writing or opening a box). They responded on a five-point Likert scale from -2 to 2 (always left, mostly left, either hand equally, mostly right, always right). Additionally, participants were asked to indicate in a single item whether they were left-or right-handed, with the option of selecting both (ambidextrous). in an alternating order throughout the session. As for the experimental tasks, the order was identical for each participant. In total, eight 1-minute resting-state EEG were recorded (order: OC-CO-OC-CO). Participants were instructed to sit quietly in a comfortable position throughout the entire recording. During the eyes-open condition, they were asked to fixate a cross in the center of the screen. Instructions to open and close their eyes were given via loudspeaker (Logitech Stereo Speakers Z120). Before moving on to the next task, the participants were instructed to open their eyes. Throughout the recording, the screen was black with white stimuli. The audio files were recorded by a female speaker and were provided to us by Nicolas Langer (University of Zurich, Switzerland).

Measures in the EEG session

Cued task-switching task

Participants conducted a parity/magnitude cued task-switching task, adapted from Sudevan et al. 39 . This task required participants to switch between two categorization tasks.

During each trial, participants had to classify the target according to one of two task-sets.

The color of the fixation cross served as the cue indicating which task-set to use. Specifically, participants had to decide whether the target, a number between 1 and 9 (except 5), was either smaller or larger than 5 (task-set magnitude, orange) or whether it was odd or even (task-set parity, violet). The cue was always valid, such that cue and target had the same color throughout all trials.

A trial consisted of a sequence of four slides. First the cue was presented for 400 to 600 ms. The cue was followed by a blank screen (ISI) for 400 to 600 ms. Then the target was presented until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms. Lastly, there was an ITI of 1000 to 1500 ms, showing again a blank screen. Presentation times were randomly selected from a uniform distribution. The duration of one trial therefore varied between 2800 and 5700 ms, depending on cue presentation time, ISI and ITI, as well as participants' reaction time (i.e., target presentation time). Participants spent on average 22 minutes on this task.

A total of 384 trials were presented. Of all trials, 50 % were switch trials, requiring a shift in the task-set, and 50 % were repeat trials, requiring the same task-set as in the trial before. Half of all trials belonged to each task-set. Condition (switch vs. repeat) and task-set (parity vs. magnitude) were fully crossed. Numbers were drawn at random with the restriction that neither task-set nor condition occurred more than three times in a row.

Furthermore, none of the targets occurred twice in a row. Mapping of response keys ("d" for odd/smaller and "l" for even/larger) was kept constant across participants.

Before starting the experimental trials, participants practiced the task, receiving feedback on the correctness of their response. The practice consisted of 10 trials for each task-set followed by 20 trials, in which both task-sets were intermixed. Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard. If participants did not respond within 3000 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice participants received the feedback "too slow".

Slides were black with either orange (#d95f02) or violet (#7570b3) stimuli, depending on the task-set. This color set makes the task accessible for people with colorblindness.

Numbers and letters were presented in typeface Arial and font size 40. All stimuli were centered horizontally and vertically.

Posner letter matching task

Participants completed a version of the Posner task 40 . This task requires participants to judge whether two letters are the same or different. Here, the target stimulus comprised two letters from the set of A, B, F, H, Q, a, b, f, h, q. Within our study, participants had to decide whether the two stimuli were semantically the same, independent of physical identity (i.e., upper or lower case). For example, Aa or AA were regarded as identical, whereas AB or bA had to be judged as different.

Within a trial, first a fixation cross was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms. Subsequently the target, comprised of two letters, was presented. The target was presented until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms.

Lastly, there was an ITI of 1000 to 1500 ms, showing a blank screen. Presentation times were randomly selected from a uniform distribution. Therefore, the duration of one trial varied between 3000 and 6000 ms, depending on fixation cross presentation time, participants' reaction time (i.e., target presentation time), as well as ITIs. Participants spent on average 7 minutes on this task.

A total of 120 trials were presented. In half of these trials, letters were different. The other half was comprised of 50 % of physically identical trials and 50 % semantically, but not physically identical trials. Letters were drawn at random with the restrictions that no combination was shown more than three times in a row and no single letter was shown more than three times in a row. In case of different letters, the order of the two selected letters was randomly chosen. Mapping of response keys ("d" for not-identical and "l" for identical) was kept constant across participants.

Before starting the experimental trials, participants practiced the task, receiving feedback on the correctness of their response. The practice consisted of 20 trials. Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard. If participants did not respond within 3000 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice, participants received the feedback "too slow".

Slides were black with white stimuli. Letters were presented in typeface Arial and font THE MAINZ NETWORK STUDY 20 size 40. All stimuli were centered horizontally and vertically.

Sternberg memory scanning task

Participants completed a version of the Sternberg memory scanning task 41, 42 . In this task, participants have to judge whether a probe stimulus did or did not appear in a sequence of five numbers. A match trial is one in which the probe is part of the sequence. A non-match is a trial in which the probe is not part of the sequence that was presented beforehand.

Within each trial, first a fixation cross was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms. Then, a sequence of five numbers was shown (each 1000 ms), interspersed by a blank screen (ISI, 400 to 1000 ms). After the last blank screen, the retention interval began (a slide with a centered question mark) and lasted for 1800 to 2200 ms. The probe digit was presented subsequently until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms. Lastly, a blank screen was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms (ITI). Temporal jittering of presentation times was drawn at random from a uniform distribution. Each trial endured between 11.8 and 18.2 seconds, depending on presentation times and participants reaction time. On average participants spent 24 minutes on the Sternberg memory scanning task.

A total of 100 trials were presented. Half of the trials were match trials, and the other half were non-match trials. Trial conditions and presented numbers were randomized with the restriction that no probe occurred twice in a row, no more than three matching or non-matching trials occurred in a row, and the position of the probe in the number sequence could not be the same three times in a row. Mapping of response keys ("d" for non-match and "l" for match) was not varied between participants.

Before starting the experimental trials, participants practiced the task, receiving feedback on the correctness of their response. The practice consisted of 20 trials. Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard. If participants did not respond within 3000 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice participants received the feedback "too slow".

Slides were black with white stimuli. Numbers were presented in typeface Arial and font size 40. All stimuli were centered horizontally and vertically.

Two-choice reaction time task

Participants conducted a simple two-choice reaction time task, adapted from the Hick paradigm 11 , in a version similar to the one used in Chen et al. 43 . In this task participants were asked to focus on a fixation cross that was flanked by a square on each side. The target, a cross, appeared either in the left or right square. Participants had to indicate with a button press on which side the target appeared. Stimulus side and response key were aligned to ensure a high level of stimulus-response compatibility. Therefore, mapping of response keys ("d" for left and "l" for right) was not varied between participants.

Trials consisted of a sequence of three slides. First a fixation cross flanked by squares was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms. Then the target stimulus appeared in one of the squares.

It was presented until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms. Lastly, there was an ITI of 1000 to 1500 ms, showing again a blank screen. Presentation times were randomly selected from a uniform distribution. The duration of one trial therefore varied between 3000 and 6000 ms, depending on fixation cross presentation time, participants' reaction time (i.e. target presentation time), as well as ITIs.

Participants spent on average 6 minutes on this task.

A total of 100 trials were presented. The plus sign appeared equally often on both sides. Trials were randomized, with the restriction that the presentation sides did not repeat more than three times in a row.

Before starting the experimental trials, participants practiced the task, receiving feedback on the correctness of their response. The practice consisted of 20 trials. Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard. If participants did not respond within 3000 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice participants received the feedback "too slow".

Slides were black with white stimuli. Stimuli were presented in typeface Arial and font size 40. The fixation cross was centered horizontally and vertically. The flanking squares had a width and height of 80 pixels and were centered 81 pixels to the left and right of the center of the screen.

Measures in the MRI session

Anatomical T1w and T2w measurements

We acquired high-resolution (0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 mm 3 isotropic resolution) anatomical T1and T2-weighted images of n = 201 individuals (one of the 202 participants who participated in the MRI session aborted the measurement during acquisition of anatomical data, see Figure 1 and Section MRI image acquisition for sequence details). For the duration of the anatomical imaging, participants viewed a short movie with nature scenes for relaxation via a mirror that was attached to the head coil. They were instructed to move the head and body as little as possible.

Adapted cued task-switching task as block design

A subset of n = 163 participants completed an MRI-adapted parity/magnitude cued task-switching paradigm in the MRI machine while we acquired multi-band multi-echo blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal data. The subset resulted from the limited scanning time of one hour per participant, as the MRI-adapted task and corresponding task-state BOLD data were collected only when time permitted. The task began at the onset of functional image acquisition (first scanner trigger), followed by an 8 s baseline interval and 12 blocks of 14 trials, totaling 168 trials. Each block lasted for approximately 39.2 s, followed by an off-period of 20.8 s. In each trial, the participants had to judge a single-digit number between 1 and 9 (excluding the number 5) according to one of two given task-sets. Which of the two task-sets had to be applied was indicated by a colored fixation cross that appeared for 400 ms before the probe stimulus. In the parity task-set (violet), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was an odd or an even number. In the magnitude task-set (orange), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was smaller or greater than 5. After an ISI of 400 ms, the probe stimulus appeared for 1500 ms. There was an ITI of 500 ms before the next trial started. Due to small delays caused by the screen's refresh rate, the timings per participant varied minimally.

Three of the task blocks were pure parity task-set blocks, three of the blocks were pure magnitude task-set blocks, and six blocks were switching blocks, in which one half of trials belonged to the parity and the other half of trials to the magnitude task-set. In addition, 50 % of trials in the switching blocks were repeat trials (previous trial belonged to the same task-set) while the other 50 % were switching trials (previous trial belonged to the other task-set). As in the cued task-switching task during the EEG measurement, numbers were drawn at random with the restriction that neither task-set nor condition occurred more than three times in a row. Participants indicated their answers via a button box using the index and middle finger of the right hand. They were instructed to press the index finger whenever the probe stimulus was even or larger than 5 and the middle finger whenever the probe stimulus was odd or smaller than 5.

Participants underwent a short training with performance feedback outside the scanner to familiarize themselves with the adapted version of the task. The practice consisted of 10 trials for each task-set followed by 4 blocks of 14 trials each, mirroring the block design participants underwent in the MRI machine. Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard ("1" with the index finger for even/larger and "2" with the middle finger for odd/smaller). If participants did not respond within 1500 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice, participants received the feedback "too slow".

Slides were dark gray (#808080) with either orange (#d95f02) or violet (#7570b3) stimuli, depending on the task-set. This color set makes the task accessible for people with colorblindness. Numbers and letters were presented in typeface Arial and font size 80. All stimuli were centered horizontally and vertically.

Resting-state fMRI: Eyes open with fixation cross

A subset of n = 157 completed ≈ 8 minutes of resting-state fMRI with a multi-band multi-echo BOLD acquisition scheme. The subset resulted due to the limited measurement time of one hour per participant. Resting-state BOLD data were only acquired if time permitted. Participants were instructed to fixate a white fixation cross on a dark gray background, to move as little as possible, and to let their mind wander without thinking of anything specific.

Diffusion-weighted imaging

We acquired diffusion-weighted images of n = 200 participants using the state-of-the-art soma and neurite density imaging (SANDI) protocol 51 that allows researchers to characterize subcellular microstructure, including soma and neurites. During the diffusion-weighted measurements, participants saw a white fixation cross on a dark gray background. They were instructed to either fixate the cross or to close their eyes, and to move as little as possible.

Amsterdam Resting-State Questionnaire 2.0

The ARSQ 2.0 44 is a retrospective self-report questionnaire designed to capture cognition and mind wandering during a resting-state fMRI measurement along 10 dimensions: discontinuity of mind, theory of mind, self, planning, sleepiness, comfort, somatic awareness, health concern, visual thought, and verbal thought. We used the German version provided by Klaus Linkenkaer-Hansen (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0184488.s001) 52.

After the last MRI measurement and after the participants had left the scanning room, they checked their answers on a sheet of paper on a 5-point Likert scale ('Completely disagree' (--) to 'Completely agree' (++)). Only participants who completed a resting-state fMRI measurement answered this questionnaire. However, one participant who completed a resting-state fMRI measurement (sub-167) did not fill in the questionnaire, resulting in n = 156 valid questionnaires.

EEG recording and quantification

EEG was continuously recorded with 60 equidistant active silver-silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrodes (EasyCap GmbH, Woerthsee, Germany). See Figure 3 for the electrode layout. Additionally, EOG was recorded by positioning one active electrode centered below the left eye (m. orbicularis oculi). All sites of EEG and EOG were referenced online to the central electrode Cz. A fronto-lateral electrode positioned equidistantly between G04 and Y10 served as ground. This position is close to F2 in the international 10-20 system 53 . We used an actiCHamp Plus amplifier with an input impedance of > 1000M Ω (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany). Recordings, in DC mode, were sampled at 1,000 Hz with a 0.05µV resolution. EEG data was recorded with the Brain Vision Recorder Version 1.25.0001 (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany). We aimed to keep the impedance of EEG electrodes below 20 kΩ (see Section EEG quality control for more details). Note. The 10-10 % electrode layout is depicted in gray in the background. Cz served as online reference. The figure was created using the Fieldtrip layout files 54 . EOG: electrooculogram, Gnd: ground, Ref : online-reference MRI image acquisition The MRI data was acquired on a 3 Tesla Magnetom Prisma scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions, Erlangen, Germany) using a 64-channel head coil for signal reception. During the data acquisition period, the MRI scanner underwent a software update from version VE11E to version syngo MR XA30. In the participants.tsv file (see Section Diffusion dataset and Section Functional dataset), we indicate which software version was used for each participant. Each measurement started with a localizer scan and an auto-align head (AAH) scout. For a subset of the participants (cf. Figure 1), we acquired functional images Additionally, six volumes without diffusion weighting were acquired anterior to posterior phase encoding direction in 18 s.

Data Record

We make the data records available in four zip archives.

The first archive (Behavioral dataset) contains all behavioral and questionnaire measures from all sessions. The second archive (EEG dataset) contains the EEG recordings from the second session and the behavioral measures gathered during that session. The third archive (Diffusion dataset) contains the anatomical T1w and T2w as well as the diffusion-weighted MRI data. The fourth archive (Functional dataset) contains the anatomical T1w and T2w data as well as the resting-state and task-state BOLD data, along with the behavioral and questionnaire measures gathered during the third session. All data is shared in its raw form. Alongside the data, we share the source code for the experimental tasks, provided there are no copyright restrictions. The archives are available in a repository from the research data centre (RDC) at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology (ZPID, https://rdc-psychology.org/en/huelsemann_jungeblut_schubert_2026).

The following sections provide details on the behavioral, EEG, and MRI data packages. See also Usage Notes for further details on how to access and process the data.

Behavioral dataset

The behavioral data from the three sessions is organized using the brain imaging data structure (BIDS) version 1.11.1 (RRID:SCR_016124) 55 . It can be accessed via a RDC-ZPID repository (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne29) at sharing level 1 for scientific use 56, 57 . The 2 for an overview of the measures.

The behavioral data structure is shown in Figure 4. General information on the dataset can be found in the file dataset_description.json, while the README file contains more detailed information on the experimental procedure and the included instruments.

Participants' demographic data (age, sex, handedness, glasses, lenses, language, education, occupation) can be assessed via the participants.tsv file in the root folder. In addition, this file lists which sessions each participant attended, the order in which they completed the sessions, the available data points, and any issues that arose during the study. It is accompanied by a .json file, giving details on the variables present in the .tsv file. The subfolder phenotype contains the assessment data from the questionnaires (Edinburgh Inventory, Amsterdam Resting State Questionnaire 2.0) as well as the raw and normalized scores for the BIS items.

Data from each instrument is provided in a single, consolidated file for all participants. There is a subfolder sub-* for each participant. We omitted the hierarchy level session, because different instruments were used in each session. Therefore, there are no repeated measurements. For each participant, the subfolder beh contains a maximum of 15 .tsv files representing 12 tasks. The files contain the item-or trial-based specifics of each experimental task (e.g. the condition), as well as the reaction times and accuracies. There are two files for each of the three complex span tasks: one containing the subtrial-based data, and an additional file containing the full recall responses (including corrected responses). In case a participant did not attend all sessions or data is missing for a specific measure, there are accordingly fewer files. The accompanying .json file details all the variables, specifying the level and possible ranges or units. It is stored at the highest hierarchy level of the data tree, as variables are identical for all participants.

We share the source code for the collection of demographic data and the experimental tasks in the subfolder code, except for the BIS and APM due to copyright restrictions. The source code for the complex span tasks can be downloaded from https://englelab.gatech.edu/translatedtasks.html#german. We additionally share stand-alone E-Run files for these tasks, which were provided by the authors of the validated German translation of the complex span tasks 46.

Figure 4

Behavioral data structure of one example participant with complete data.

Note. Participant data is organized into the subfolders according to the BIDS format: beh (task responses).

EEG dataset

The electrophysiological data, recorded in the EEG session, is organized using the BIDS 55 with the extension for EEG data 58 . The data can be downloaded from a RDC-ZPID repository (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne06). It also contains trial-based accuracies and reaction times for the tasks conducted in the EEG session (cf. Table 2), as well as source code for the experimental tasks (cf. section Behavioral dataset). The data is provided under sharing level 2 for restricted scientific use 56, 57 . EEG data are not regarded as potentially identifiable biometric data. However the potential for re-identification at some point cannot be entirely precluded. Therefore, access to the data is restricted. Data users must agree not to attempt any re-identification, and data is only shared with identifiable persons who have a specific research question and sign a standardized data user agreement.

The electrophysiological data structure is shown in Figure 5. General information on the dataset is provided with the dataset_description.json file. The experimental procedure and a short description of all experimental tasks are described in the README file.

Participant characteristics regarding age, sex, handedness, laterality quotient of handedness (calculated using the Edinburgh Inventory by) 34 , and glasses/lenses, are provided in the participants.tsv file in the root folder. Additionally, this file contains information on which sessions each participant attended, the order in which they completed them, the available data points and any issues that arose during the EEG session. The variables and their levels are defined in the file participants.json. The coordsystem.json file defines the coordinate system and units used to describe the positions of electrodes. The auditory instructions for the resting-state EEG are provided as .wav files in the stimuli subfolder.

There is a subfolder sub-* for each participant. As there was only one EEG session per participant, the hierarchy level session was omitted in the data structure. We share the source code for the experimental tasks in the subfolder code.

Furthermore we share the scripts needed to reproduce the quality-control metrics and manuscript figures and a standard preprocessing script for EEG data. The latter script can be applied to raw data to produce minimally processed, cleaned, continuous datasets. Note. Participant data is organized into the subfolders according to the BIDS format: beh (task responses), eeg (electrophysiological recordings).

MRI data

The de-identified MRI data is provided under sharing level 2 for restricted scientific use 56, 57 because the potential for re-identification at some point cannot be entirely precluded.

Data users must agree not to attempt any re-identification, and data is only shared with identifiable persons who have a specific research question and sign a standardized data user agreement.

Diffusion dataset

The structural T1w, T2w, and diffusion-weighted MRI data, recorded in the MRI session, are organized in accordance with BIDS 55 . The data can be downloaded from a RDC-ZPID repository (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne01). It also contains code for reproducing the MRI quality control metrics (cf. section MRI quality control).

The diffusion MRI dataset structure is shown in Figure 6. The file dataset_description.json contains meta-data on the dataset. We provide data on participant age, sex, the laterality quotient of handedness (calculated using the Edinburgh Inventory by) 34 , and whether data was collected before or after the scanner software upgrade and the T2w protocol change in the participants.tsv file. Additionally, this file contains information on the order in which participants completed the three sessions and any issues that arose during the MRI session. The variable definitions are documented in the participants.json file. The experimental procedure and a brief description of all experimental tasks for the MRI session are provided in the README file.

For each participant who took part in a T1w, T2w, or diffusion-weighted measurement, the defaced T1w, T2w, and raw diffusion-weighted data is provided. Defacing was performed using fsl_deface in FSL version 6.0.7.6 59 . Additionally, we removed any potentially identifiable information from MRI data headers such as location, date, and time of measurement. Defacing failed for the T2w data of one participant (sub-075) and consequently, we do not share the T2w data of this individual. There are subfolders for each participant containing the files of the anatomical measurements (anat) and the diffusion-weighted data (dwi). As there was only one MRI session per participant, the hierarchy level session was omitted in the data structure.

In the subfolder code, we provide the scripts needed to reproduce the MRI quality-control metrics and Figure 9. Note. Participant data is organized into the subfolders according to the BIDS format: anat (T1-and T2-weighted data) and dwi (diffusion-weighted data).

Functional dataset

All files contained in the functional MRI dataset are organized in accordance with BIDS 55 . The data can be downloaded from a RDC-ZPID repository (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne02). It also contains trial-based accuracies and reaction times for the task-switching task conducted during the MRI measurement as well as source code for the task.

The functional MRI dataset structure is shown in Figure 7. Like the diffusion MRI dataset, the functional MRI dataset contains the file dataset_description.json with meta-data on the dataset, participants.* files, and a README file.

For each participant who took part in a resting-state or task-based BOLD measurement, the defaced anatomical T1w, T2w, and raw BOLD data is provided. We removed any potentially identifiable information from MRI data headers, such as location, date, and time of measurement. There are subfolders for each participant containing the files of the anatomical measurements (anat), the functional BOLD data (resting-state, task-based, func), the behavioral data (task responses, beh), and the spin-echo fieldmaps (fmap). As there was only one MRI session per participant, the hierarchy level session was omitted in the data structure.

If participants completed the task-switching task in the MRI machine, the individual starting times and durations of all experimental blocks are saved in the *_events.tsv file in the func subfolder. This file can be used for block definition in general linear model (GLM) analyses. Unfortunately, this file was overwritten and could not be restored for one participant (sub-124). The columns of the *_events.tsv are the same for all participants and defined in the *_events.json at the highest hierarchy level of the data tree. Detailed behavioral data from the switching task is saved in the *_beh.tsv file in the beh subdirectory. Unfortunately, this file was overwritten and could not be restored for one participant (sub-053). The columns of the *_beh.tsv are the same for all participants and defined in the *_beh.json at the highest hierarchy level of the data tree.

If participants completed a resting-state fMRI measurement, they filled in the ARSQ 2.0 after the last measurement and after they left the MRI scanner room. The questionnaire data from the ARSQ 2.0 is saved in a single file (arsq.tsv) in the phenotype subdirectory for all participants. Unfortunately, one participant did not fill in the ARSQ 2.0 (sub-167). The columns of the arsq.tsv are defined in the arsq.json in the phenotype subdirectory.

In the subfolder code, we provide fMRIPrep 60 and tedana 61 scripts exemplary for the resting-state BOLD data. These scripts can be used to run multi-echo independent component analysis (ICA) and to obtain the denoised optimally combined timeseries of the functional rest and task data that can be used for further analysis. We also share the source code for the experimental task conducted during the task-based BOLD measurement. Note. Participant data is organized into the subfolders according to the BIDS format: anat (T1-and T2-weighted data), beh (task responses), fmap (spin-echo fieldmaps), func (task-based and resting-state BOLD data and task events).

Technical Validation

By structuring the data in accordance with BIDS and depositing it in the RDC-ZPID repository, we ensure that our data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, i.e. highly FAIR-compliant (https://go-fair.org/fair-principles/) 62 , facilitating broad and efficient reuse by the research community.

Quality control of behavioral recordings

The data was checked for completeness. We provide raw, non-aggregated data. Only valid datasets are included in the data record. The participants.tsv file reports any relevant issues, which might lead to the decision to exclude a dataset. In case a task was interrupted and restarted due to technical problems, only the valid trials are provided. The provided data adheres to the BIDS format, as confirmed by the BIDS validator 3.0.0-alpha.3. Behavioral data (reaction time, accuracy) is accompanied by trial characteristics, such as the presented stimuli, presentation times, or condition.

The BIS was conducted by one of three trained experimenters. Before receiving formal training, each experimenter first participated in a session led by an experienced experimenter.

Subsequently, each experimenter assisted in at least one session, and later led at least one session under the experienced experimenter's supervision. Because the training always included the entire behavioral session, all experimenters were familiar with the instructions for every task. Similarly, experimenters were trained and practiced the procedure for the EEG and MRI sessions. Experimenters responded to participants' questions, ensuring that the wording remained as similar as possible to that of the standardized task instructions.

Questionnaire and experimental data were directly and automatically collected via computerized experimental tasks. Only the BIS and the ARSQ 2.0, being paper-and-pencil tests, required a manual evaluation. The manual evaluation of the BIS was conducted by two trained, independent raters in accordance with the test manual. All tasks related to the operation-specific components processing capacity, processing speed, and memory were scored by one rater using scoring templates. A second independent rater performed random spot checks. If the error rate exceeded 2 %, a complete second evaluation was conducted by the independent rater. Any remaining discrepancies were resolved by an experienced researcher who supervised the manual evaluation. All tasks related to the creativity component were fully double-rated. Any remaining discrepancies were again resolved by an experienced researcher.

The participants.tsv file reports any issues that occurred during the sessions and that might be relevant for data analysis. In particular, the data of sub-027 from the complex span tasks is not shared, as the participant did not adhere to the task instructions. The participant reported that they had circumvented the time limit for the processing component by waiting before answering in the second exercise block. The time limits for this participant were 11.9 s for the operation span, 16.5 s for the reading span, and 26.5 s for the symmetry span. None of the other participants reported such a strategy, but there are participants with equally high time limits. Furthermore, due to a technical problem, no data is available for sub-171 for the reading span task. Behavioral data from the continuous cued task-switching task should not be used for three participants (sub-041, sub-164, sub-189) who did not adhere to the task instructions. For example, they only followed one task rule during parts of the task, instead of switching between both task rules. Data from another participant (sub-190) needs to be used with caution due to low overall accuracy. Furthermore, behavioral data from the MRI-adapted cued task-switching task should not be used for one participant (sub-032) who did not adhere to the task instructions. This participant has missing answers on 50% of all trials and an overall accuracy rate of only 2.3%. Additionally, data from the MRI-adapted cued task-switching task of an additional 23 participants (sub-062, sub-076, sub-095, sub-096, sub-129, sub-147, sub-151, sub-160, sub-165, sub-172, sub-174, sub-180, sub-184, sub-188, sub-190, sub-194, sub-195, sub-205, sub-211, sub-212, sub-213, sub-214, sub-215) should be used with caution. These participants had accuracies < 55%, suggesting they might not have adhered fully to the task instructions. Note that all of the above participants who had accuracies < 55% were among the last 40 individuals who participated in the MRI measurement. Thus, these individuals clustered in a couple of measurement sessions. Possibly, changes in the experimenter who gave verbal instructions to the participants have influenced these participants' accuracies. We rule out the possibility of a technical defect of the button box because the button box was tested before each measurement by the participant and the response mapping was checked by the experimenter. Furthermore, for the ARSQ 2.0 one participant had more than 75 % missing responses. Two further participants missed about one third of the responses.

Reliabilities for all questionnaire and behavioral data are listed in Table 2 for the current sample. Reliability estimates are based on Cronbach's α 63 in case of questionnaire data and the cognitive ability test APM. For the BIS we report McDonald's total ω t 64 because it does not assume tau-equivalence. Therefore it captures the varying contributions of the manifest indicators to the latent general cognitive ability factor, providing a more accurate reliability estimate than Cronbach's α. We extracted only one factor, because the short form of the BIS only allows to extract a general cognitive ability score and does not contain enough items to model the sub-factors that are present in the full version. For the experimental tasks Spearman-Brown corrected 65, 66 split-half correlations are reported for accuracies (binding and complex span tasks) or reaction times (cued-task switching, Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). We did not exclude interindividual outliers in order to show the reliabilities of the tasks in the whole data record. Nevertheless, participants who did not adhere to task instruction were excluded. This was the case for one participant in the complex span tasks, three participants in the cued task-switching task in the EEG session, and one participant in the cued task-switching task in the MRI session. Data users need to refer to the participant.tsv file in order to determine whether particular datasets should be excluded for a specific task. For reliabilities of reaction time data (cued-task switching, Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time), intra-individual outliers, defined as reaction times falling more than 3 SD above or below the participants mean, were excluded. Across all tasks and participants, the proportion of outlier trials ranged from 0.00 to 4.44 %.

EEG quality control

The data is complete for all participants that took part in the EEG session (N = 212).

However, the data from the cued task-switching task should not be used or used with caution for four participants who did not adhere to the task instructions or had overall low accuracies as described in Section Quality control of behavioral recordings. Details can be found in the participants.tsv file. The provided data adheres to the BIDS format, as confirmed by the BIDS validator v3.0.0-alpha.3.

EEG was recorded in a dimly-lit, electrically shielded, sound-attenuated recording cabin. No electrical devices or personal belongings were allowed in the cabin during the execution of tasks.

Before starting the recording, it was ensured that the impedance values of electrodes were sufficiently low and as uniform as possible. Several minutes passed between the completion of the EEG preparations and the commencement of the tasks, allowing the connection between scalp and electrodes to further settle. Impedance values for EEG electrodes at the beginning of the recording were on average at 4.4 kΩ (SD = 3.5 kΩ, median = 4, range = 0-43). For all but nine participants (96 %), initial impedance values for EEG electrodes were kept below 20 kΩ. Impedance values for reference and ground were on average at 2.7 kΩ (SD = 2.5 kΩ, median = 2, range = 0-14). Impedance for the EOG channel was on average at 13.9 kΩ (SD = 10.9 kΩ, median = 12, range = 1-69). Impedance values for the EOG channel for all but 45 participants (79 %) were kept below 20 kΩ, while 2 participants (< 1 %) had impedance values above 50 kΩ. For one participant, impedance values between the second and third task are reported, due to technical reasons.

Before starting the recording, participants received a brief introduction to EEG, while being able to monitor their own recording. Participants were shown how head and body movements can result in EEG artifacts. Thereafter, participants were instructed to find a comfortable sitting position and move as little as possible during the tasks. They were informed to use the breaks to stretch or change their position. Furthermore, participants were instructed to focus on the center of the screen, as all tasks would be presented in a centered manner. Moreover, participants were instructed not to suppress blinks and to maintain their natural blinking pattern.

In order to guarantee optimal data quality, the preparation of electrodes, impedance checks, and visual data inspection were overseen by an experienced experimenter. This experiment supervisor was available throughout the recording sessions and contacted whenever questions arose during data recording. One experimenter monitored the recording throughout the session. In case of excessive movements, the experimenter reminded the participant of the importance of remaining in a relaxed position. This reminder was given in between the tasks or after practicing a task. Furthermore, in case an electrode became detached from the head surface, electrodes were readjusted during short breaks in between tasks, without stopping the measurement. The participants.tsv file contains information which participants underwent re-adjustment.

We provide raw, non-processed EEG data. To give an impression of the data quality, THE MAINZ NETWORK STUDY 40 calculated the spectra in EEGLAB v2025.1.0 67 on the raw data without any preprocessing 898 using the function pop_spectopo.m with 100 % of the data. Note. Single participant EEG spectra (thin lines) are shown together with the mean spectrum (thick line, N = 212). Spectra were calculated on non-processed, raw data.

MRI quality control 900

An overview of the completeness of the MRI data is provided in Figure 1. Complete 901 DWI and structural T1w and T2w data is available for n = 200 participants. Resting-state fMRI data is available for n = 157 participants and task-based fMRI data, including behavioral data and events files, is available for n = 161 participants. However, functional MRI data from the MRI-adapted cued task-switching task should not be used or used with caution for several participants who did not adhere to the task instructions or had overall low accuracies as described in Section Quality control of behavioral recordings. Details can be found in the participants.tsv file. Reliabilities for all questionnaire and behavioral data of the MRI session are listed in Table 2. The provided data adheres to the BIDS format, as confirmed by the BIDS validator v3.0.1.

Participants were positioned in the MRI machine using cushions to stabilize the head within the head coil and to minimize head motion. In addition, all participants were instructed to move as little as possible during the measurement.

Post measurement, we assessed the quality of the structural T1-and T2-weighted images (Figure 9A and 9B) using MRIQC version 24.0.2 68 . We analyzed the coefficient of joint variation (CJV) of gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) and the entropy focus criterion (EFC) to assess the presence of artifacts and blurring or ghosting caused by head motion. Higher values of CJV and EFC indicate increased artifact contamination and reduced image quality, whereas lower values reflect better data quality. Both distributions were clustered tightly and relatively low with few outliers, suggesting generally good quality with minimal motion artifacts. We also assessed the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF), GM, and WM to evaluate the quality of signal in each tissue type. As expected, SNR was highest in GM and WM compared to CSF.

We checked the diffusion-weighted images' quality by inspecting the root mean squared (RMS) voxel-wise displacement (obtained from FSL's eddy) relative to the first volume across all volumes, averaged across participants (Figure 9C). A gradual increase of the RMS voxel-wise displacement was apparent over time, suggesting increasing fatigue or discomfort towards the end of the measurement. Still, RMS remains under 1.5 mm, indicating acceptable overall quality.

To assess the quality of the multi-band multi-echo functional resting-state and task-based BOLD images, we first processed the individual echoes using fMRIPrep 60 and then created the optimally combined resting-state and task echoes per participant using tedana. We computed the average framewise displacement (FD) of the optimally combined resting-state and task echoes (Figure 9). Most FD values stayed below 0.1 mm with only few outliers 934 displaying higher motion. Overall, both resting-state and task-based images show an excellent 935 motion profile.

Complex span tasks

The complex span tasks are a set of working memory tasks that require participants to store information and recall it in the correct order at a later stage 47 . Between storage and recall, participants perform an intervening processing task. In this study, we used the German version of three complex span tasks 46 . Participants completed the operation span, the reading span, and the symmetry span task, with the order of the tasks being the same for each participant.

In the operation span task, participants were presented with three to seven processing tasks, each followed by a letter that had to be retained in the correct order of their presentation. The letters were presented for 800 ms each. The recall test comprised of a 4 x 3 matrix containing all possible letters. Participants were instructed to click on the previously presented letters in the correct serial order. There was the possibility to click on a 'blank' button whenever the participant could not recall one letter at a certain position. Participants could also clear all the letters they had already entered to correct their entries. In the operation span task, the processing task consisted of math problems followed by a number (e.g., '(7 × 3) -3 =?' followed by '18'). Participants had to judge whether the presented number was the correct solution for the math problem or not. There were 15 trials in total.

The reading span task was similar in structure to the operation span task but participants had to judge whether a given sentence was semantically meaningful or not as the processing task. Again, three to seven processing tasks each followed by a letter were presented per trial and there were 15 trials in total.

In the symmetry span task, participants were presented with two to five geometric figures that they had to judge as either symmetrical or not as a processing task. After each geometrical figure, a highlighted screen position in a 4 x 4 matrix was presented that participants were instructed to store. In the recall test, participants saw an empty 4 x 4 matrix and were asked to click the previously highlighted screen positions in the correct serial order. There were 12 trials in total.

All three complex span tasks were preceded by three blocks of practice trials. In the first block participants practiced only the storage component (remembering and recalling a letter or a highlighted screen position in the correct serial position) in two trials with set size 2 and two trials with set size 3. In the second block (15 trials), they practiced only the

Usage Notes

Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data archives can be downloaded from the RDC-ZPID repository (https://rdc-psychology.org/en/huelsemann_jungeblut_schubert_2026). Additional information on how to access data from the ZPID is provided on their https://rdc-psychology.org/en/reuse-data/access-data.

All data archives are organized using BIDS (https://bids.neuroimaging.io). Therefore, all provided variables are described in accompanying .json files. The archives also comprise meta-data on the study (dataset_description.json) and an overview of the experimental procedure (README). Furthermore, the RDC-ZPID repository provides a comprehensive overview of all provided variables, facilitating access to these data. The file participants.tsv, which accompanies each data archive, contains an overview, which data points are available and valid for each participant. Any issues arising during the study are also listed in that file. This file should be reviewed before conducting any data analysis.

When using data from the Mainz Network Study, this publication should be cited in addition to the respective data repository (Behavior DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne29 EEG DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne06 diffusion MRI DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne01 functional MRI DOI: https://doi.org/10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne02). and neuroimaging data (DOI: 10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne01 for structural and 10.5160/psychdata.hnme25ne02 for functional data). However, for BIS and APM neither stimulus material nor source code can be shared due to copyright restrictions. The source code for the complex span tasks can be downloaded from https://englelab.gatech.edu/translatedtasks.html#german. Additionally, stand-alone E-Run files are provided for the complex span tasks in the behavioral data archive.

The scripts needed to reproduce the quality-control metrics and manuscript figures are provided in the Open Science Framework repository at https://osf.io/9ekbr as well as in the subfolder code within each of the data archives. Furthermore, we provide standard preprocessing scripts for EEG and MRI data in the code subfolder of the EEG and MRI data archives. These scripts can be applied to raw data to produce minimally processed, cleaned, continuous datasets.

For each participant, the subfolder eeg contains 33 files each. The *_electrodes.tsv contains the recorded channels, their cartesian coordinates, electrode material, and the impedance measurement values recorded at the beginning of the session. The corresponding .json-file can be found in the root directory. Furthermore, the folder contains files of the four resting EEG measurements and the four recordings during the execution of the four tasks (cued-task switching task (continuous design), Posner letter matching task, Sternberg memory scanning task, two-choice reaction time task). Four files are provided for each recording, comprised of channel information (*_channel.tsv), event marker latencies (*_event.tsv), the raw EEG data (*_eeg.set), and EEG measurement information (*_eeg.json). The subfolder beh contains four files containing the trial details and behavioral responses for the four experimental tasks conducted in the EEG session. The root folder contains the event marker information (*_event.json) and variable definitions for behavioral data (*_beh.json).
